facts.statement: The genus Tropeognathus was described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1987.
facts.quote: authority: Wellnhofer, 1987

facts.statement: Fossils of Tropeognathus date to the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous (Albian),

facts.statement: Tropeognathus lived in South America during the late Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Tropeognathus (meaning "keel jaw") is a genus of large pterosaurs from the late Early Cretaceous of South America.

facts.statement: Fossils of Tropeognathus were found in the Romualdo Formation within the Santana Group in northeastern Brazil.
facts.quote: Fossil remains of Tropeognathus have been recovered from the Romualdo Formation, which is a Lagerstätte located in the Santana Group of the Araripe Basin in northeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer named the type species Tropeognathus mesembrinus in 1987.
facts.quote: In 1987, it was named and described as the type species Tropeognathus mesembrinus by Peter Wellnhofer.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen BSP 1987 I 46 dates to the latest Aptian and earliest Albian stages.
facts.quote: The holotype, BSP 1987 I 46, was discovered in a layer of the Romualdo Formation within the Santana Group, dating to the latest Aptian and earliest Albian stages.

facts.statement: In 2013, Alexander Kellner referred specimen MN 6594-1, a nearly complete skeleton, to Tropeognathus.
facts.quote: In 2013, Brazilian paleontologist Alexander Kellner referred a third, larger, specimen: MN 6594-1, a skeleton with skull, with extensive elements of all body parts, except the tail and the lower hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Tropeognathus is classified within the family Anhangueridae, though some studies place it in Ornithocheiridae.
facts.quote: This genus is considered to be a member of the family Anhangueridae, but several studies have also recovered it within another family called Ornithocheiridae.

facts.statement: Recent analyses in 2019 and 2020 place Tropeognathus in the subfamily Tropeognathinae within Anhangueridae, as a sister taxon to Siroccopteryx.
facts.quote: many subsequent analyses made in 2019 and 2020 have recovered Tropeognathus within the family Anhangueridae, with a specific one by Borja Holgado and Rubi Pêgas in 2020, placing Tropeognathus more specifically within the subfamily Tropeognathinae, sister taxon to Siroccopteryx.

facts.statement: Tropeognathus is considered the largest pterosaur found in the Southern Hemisphere, with an estimated wingspan of about 8.5 meters.
facts.quote: With an estimated wingspan around 8.5 m, Tropeognathus is regarded as the largest pterosaur found in the Southern Hemisphere, only rivaled by the huge azhdarchids.

facts.statement: The maximum estimated wingspan for Tropeognathus is 8.70 meters, significantly larger than its close relatives which range from 4.5 to 6.1 meters.
facts.quote: The maximum wingspan estimate for Tropeognathus reaches 8.70 m, making it slightly larger than the average estimate for the genus, though much larger than other close relatives such as Ornithocheirus and Coloborhynchus, which are typically estimated to be between 4.5 to 6.1 m.

facts.statement: Tropeognathus possessed distinctively convex, keeled crests on the tip of its upper snout and a smaller mass on the underside of its lower jaws.
facts.quote: The skull of Tropeognathus bore a distinctively convex, "keeled" crests on the lower end of its snout, with an opposing, smaller mass on the underside of the lower jaws.

facts.statement: The upper crest of Tropeognathus extended from the snout tip back to the large opening on the side of the skull.
facts.quote: The upper crests arose from the snout tip and extended back to the fenestra nasoantorbitalis, the large opening in the skull side.

facts.statement: Tropeognathus has a broader skull than its relatives because its upper jaw crest is more prominent and much larger.
facts.quote: The jaws can be distinguished from its relatives by a few differences in the crest: unlike its close relatives Coloborhynchus and Ornithocheirus, the crest on the upper jaw of Tropeognathus was more prominent and much larger, and therefore resulting in a broader skull.

facts.statement: Later scientific analysis revised the maximum estimated wingspan of the large specimen used in media to 8.70 meters.
facts.quote: The final description of the remains found a maximum estimated wingspan of 8.70 m for this large specimen.

facts.statement: In 2013, specimen MN 6594-V was identified as the largest known individual pterosaur based on its completeness.
facts.quote: Nevertheless, specimen MN 6594-V in 2013 was, at its degree of completeness, the largest known pterosaur individual.

facts.statement: Researchers have debated the validity of Tropeognathus, often reassigning its fossils to other genera like Anhanguera or Ornithocheirus.
facts.quote: After Tropeognathus mesembrinus was named by Peter Wellnhofer in 1987, other researchers tended to consider it part of several other genera, leading to an enormous taxonomic confusion.

facts.statement: In 2013, researchers concluded that Tropeognathus is a valid genus containing only the species T. mesembrinus.
facts.quote: In 2013 however, Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner concluded Tropeognathus to be valid, and containing only T. mesembrinus, the type species.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding family classification, with some European researchers preferring to place Tropeognathus in Ornithocheiridae rather than Anhangueridae.
facts.quote: This concept is mostly used by the European colleagues, who prefer to use the Ornithocheiridae as the most inclusive group rather than the Anhangueridae.

facts.statement: The genus Tropeognathus belongs to the subfamily Tropeognathinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Tropeognathinae

facts.statement: The genus Tropeognathus was named by Wellnhofer in 1987.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Wellnhofer, 1987

facts.quote: Fue un miembro de la familia Ornithocheiridae (también conocida como Anhangueridae)

facts.statement: T. mesembrinus had distinctive convex keel-shaped crests on its snout and the underside of its lower jaw.
facts.quote: T. mesembrinus tenía unas distintivas crestas convexas, en forma de quilla sobre su hocico y en el envés de la mandíbula inferior

facts.statement: The first five dorsal vertebrae were fused into a structure called a notarium.
facts.quote: Las primeras cinco vértebras dorsales están fusionadas en una estructura denominada notarium

facts.statement: Five sacral vertebrae were fused into a synsacrum.

facts.statement: The genus name Tropeognathus is derived from the Greek words for keel and jaw.
facts.quote: El nombre del género se deriva del griego τρόπις, tropis, "quilla", y γνάθος, gnathos, "mandíbula"

facts.statement: The species name mesembrinus is derived from the Greek for 'from the south', referring to its origin in the Southern Hemisphere.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie se deriva del koiné mesembrinos, "del mediodía", "del sur", en referencia a su procedencia del hemisferio sur

facts.statement: The holotype BSP 1987 I 46 was found in the Romualdo Member of the Santana Formation, dating to the Aptian-Albian.
facts.quote: El holotipo, BSP 1987 I 46, fue descubierto en una capa del Miembro Romualdo de la Formación Santana, que data del Aptiense-Albiense

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer named and described the type species Tropeognathus mesembrinus in 1987.

facts.statement: In 2013, Taissa Rodrigues and Kellner concluded that Tropeognathus is a valid genus.

facts.statement: Wellnhofer named a second species, Tropeognathus robustus, in 1987.
facts.quote: En 1987 Wellnhofer nombró a una segunda especie, Tropeognathus robustus

facts.statement: The specimen MN 6594-V is the largest relatively complete pterosaur individual known.
facts.quote: Aun así, el espécimen MN 6594-V es el individuo de pterosaurio relativamente completo más grande que se conoce

facts.statement: Tropeognathus lived between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago during the Aptian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (119.57 to 113.2 million years ago)

rejected.statement: A 2006 BBC book incorrectly claimed that a specimen related to Tropeognathus had a wingspan of 12 meters and weighed 100 kilograms.
rejected.quote: In Walking with Dinosaurs: A Natural History, a companion book to the series, it was claimed that several large bone fragments from the Santana Group (known as Santana Formation in the book) of Brazil had indicated that O. mesembrinus may have had a wingspan reaching 12 m and a weight of 100 kg, making it one of the largest known pterosaurs.

rejected.statement: A book accompanying the Walking with Dinosaurs series claimed that bone fragments from the Santana Formation indicated Tropeognathus could reach a wingspan of nearly 12 meters and weigh 100 kilograms.
rejected.quote: En Walking with Dinosaurs: A Natural History, un libro complementario de la serie, se afirma que varios grandes fragmentos de hueso de la formación Santana de Brasil indican que Tropeognathus puede haber alcanzado una envergadura de casi 12 metros y un peso de cien kilogramos
